title: T1531 — Account Access Removal
subtitle: Interactive walkthrough of Account Access Removal with the technique-specific attack path and defender evidence.

steps.title: 1 · Stolen credentials
steps.caption: The attacker holds a domain-admin password stolen in a phishing campaign two days earlier. No account changes have happened yet, so the SIEM is quiet. The only early signal is the phishing report itself - which is why reporting culture matters
steps.defender: IdP and SaaS audit logs record token issuance, consent, sign-in location and API access.

steps.title: 2 · RDP logon to the domain controller
steps.caption: From the shared admin workstation ADM-WKS-04, the attacker opens a Remote Desktop (RDP) session to DC01 at 03:12 local time. Evidence: Event 4624 with Logon Type 10, plus 4672 "special privileges assigned" for the admin account. Few people ever RDP into a domain controller, and almost never at that hour
steps.defender: IdP and SaaS audit logs record token issuance, consent, sign-in location and API access.

steps.title: 3 · Password resets
steps.caption: The attacker resets the passwords of six admin and service accounts in four minutes, DEADWOOD-style - each password becomes a long random value only the attacker knows. Evidence: six 4724 events sharing one SubjectUserName within the same session
steps.defender: IdP and SaaS audit logs record token issuance, consent, sign-in location and API access.

steps.title: 4 · Security accounts disabled
steps.caption: Next, nine security-team and admin accounts are disabled, so analysts cannot log in to investigate. Evidence: a burst of 4725 events from the same subject. This step is why the SOC must alert on disables, not only on deletions
steps.defender: IdP and SaaS audit logs record token issuance, consent, sign-in location and API access.

steps.title: 5 · Admin accounts deleted
steps.caption: The attacker deletes four accounts, including two administrator accounts - the Akira pattern, performed right before encryption in real cases. Evidence: 4726 events, each recording the SubjectUserName of the stolen admin. That field names the attacker's path
steps.defender: IdP and SaaS audit logs record token issuance, consent, sign-in location and API access.

steps.title: 6 · Lockout storm
steps.caption: The attacker deliberately types wrong passwords against the remaining admin accounts. After repeated failures, account lockout policy kicks in: fourteen 4740 lockout events appear in ten minutes, all from the same source workstation. The remaining admins are now locked too
steps.defender: IdP and SaaS audit logs record token issuance, consent, sign-in location and API access.

steps.title: 7 · Cloud identity sabotage
steps.caption: In parallel, the attacker uses a stolen Global Admin session in the cloud identity provider. They remove MFA factors from admins and deactivate the break-glass account. Evidence: Entra ID audit records such as "Delete user" and "User deleted security info" - the LAPSUS$ pattern of locking an organization out of all access
steps.defender: IdP and SaaS audit logs record token issuance, consent, sign-in location and API access.

steps.title: 8 · SOC contains and recovers
steps.caption: The SIEM correlates the 4724 + 4725 + 4726 burst into one critical incident. The SOC revokes attacker sessions, blocks the source, activates the second break-glass account, and restores accounts and MFA settings from the identity configuration backup. Recovery time depends entirely on the quality of that backup and runbook
